text:
evelyn: Hey — running into TLS verify failures from our Java SDK when opening streaming WS connections to our Redwood Private endpoint from a K8s pod behind the corp TLS proxy. Error is a PKIX path building failure.

sam (sdk): Can you paste the stacktrace and the command you used to start the container? Quick guess: Java's truststore vs OS CA file mismatch.

evelyn: Stacktrace (abridged):
```
javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: PKIX path building failed: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target
  at sun.security.ssl.SSLContextImpl$TLSContext.con$etc...
```
Started container with default openjdk:11-jre image. We tried adding the corp CA to /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt in the image and re-running, but the JVM still fails. We also tried `-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=/etc/ssl/corp-trust.jks -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit` but streaming connection still errors. Non-streaming HTTP calls using okhttp3 succeed to the same host in the same pod. Streaming (websocket) fails. :confused:

sam (sdk): That detail is useful — if non-streaming HTTP works but websocket fails, the SDK's streaming stack (okhttp websocket layer) might be creating its own SSLContext or using a different socket factory. Can you run `openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <host>:443 -servername <host>` from the pod and paste the chain? Also check the JVM cacerts content: `keytool -list -keystore $JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts -storepass changeit | grep -i CorpName`

mike (eng-infra): +1 to sam. Also, corp MITM proxies sometimes perform TLS interception and then do mTLS to upstreams; they may rewrite/terminate client certs which breaks mutual TLS flows. A couple of quick checks: 1) curl from the pod with `--cacert /etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem` to validate the intercepted cert chain; 2) openssl s_client to see issuer chain. Example commands: 
```bash
# inspect chain
openssl s_client -showcerts -connect redwood-private.example.internal:443 -servername redwood-private.example.internal

# import corp CA into a JKS truststore
keytool -import -alias corp-root -file /tmp/corp-ca.pem -keystore /etc/ssl/corp-trust.jks -storepass changeit -noprompt
```
If curl + `--cacert` works but the JVM still fails, the runtime trust store likely isn't picked up by the streaming client.

jenna (security): Quick policy note: do NOT recommend disabling certificate verification as a workaround. We should either: a) add the corp internal CA to the JVM truststore used in our base images and rotate it via image updates, or b) work with infra to allow egress passthrough for redwood-private endpoints so the proxy doesn't MITM that traffic. If there's mTLS involved, the proxy can strip/replace client certs which will break mutual auth.

evelyn: Good call — we do use mTLS for Private: clients present certs. I wonder if the proxy is stripping client certs on the websocket handshake which explains why non-mTLS HTTP works but streaming fails. What should we do short-term to unblock dev pods?

sam (sdk): Short-term options (ranked):
1) Have infra add an egress allowlist for *.redwood-private.example.internal so the proxy doesn't intercept that traffic (preferred).
2) Add corp CA to the JRE cacerts inside the pod image (we can automate in CI) — then websocket should trust the proxy cert.
3) As a last-resort dev-only workaround, allow configuring a custom SSLContext/truststore path in the Java SDK builder (so devs can point to /etc/ssl/corp-trust.jks). I can open a PR to expose `.sslContext(...)` / `.trustStorePath(...)` in the SDK, and add better error messages when PKIX failures occur (include server cert subject/issuer and which truststore was checked).

sam (sdk): Example Java snippet for creating an SSLContext from a JKS and wiring into OkHttp: 
```java
KeyStore ks = KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType());
try (InputStream is = Files.newInputStream(Paths.get("/etc/ssl/corp-trust.jks"))) {
  ks.load(is, "changeit".toCharArray());
}
TrustManagerFactory tmf = TrustManagerFactory.getInstance(TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm());
tmf.init(ks);
SSLContext sslContext = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS");
sslContext.init(null, tmf.getTrustManagers(), null);
OkHttpClient client = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .sslSocketFactory(sslContext.getSocketFactory(), (X509TrustManager)tmf.getTrustManagers()[0])
    .build();
```
This will get the websocket layer to use the corp truststore. I'll add tests.

mike (eng-infra): I'll spin up an infra ticket to add an egress bypass for redwood-private for the affected namespace(s) so we can test without interception. Ticket: INFRA-2047 (I'll add details + link). If we opt to update base images with corp CA, also open an image-build ticket.

jenna (security): If infra does an allowlist, include a short review by Security so we confirm no sensitive traffic is bypassing required controls. Otherwise image changes must go through the normal CVE/scan pipeline.

evelyn: Thanks — action items:
- @mike (eng-infra) INFRA-2047: create egress bypass so redwood-private endpoints are not MITM'd.
- @sam (sdk) please open PR to expose SSLContext/trustStorePath + better PKIX error logging.
- @jenna (security) we will coordinate on policy for allowlist vs image update.

sam (sdk): I'll open the PR today and include a small integration test that fails when the custom truststore is not present. Pinging codeowners for a quick review. 

evelyn: Great. If anyone hits this locally in the meantime, quick dev workaround: `keytool -import -trustcacerts -alias corp-root -file corp-ca.pem -keystore $JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts -storepass changeit` inside your dev container image. Not ideal but works for local repro.

jenna (security): :thumbsup: please tag me on PR & INFRA ticket.

mike (eng-infra): INFRA-2047 created, link: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/INFRA-2047 :eyes:

evelyn: Thanks all — I'll wait on INFRA-2047 and sam's PR before updating the platform docs.
